I. Overview
The paper offers a valuable literature review on Text and Data Mining (TDM), mapping the
complex regulatory framework surrounding these processes and shedding light on what
constitutes lawful TDM. However, several areas require improvement for the paper to reach its full
potential. This report provides some comments and suggestions to strengthen the paper's
structure, argumentation, and use of sources.
II. Comments
1) Introduction
○

○

Structure improvement: The introduction could be better structured to present the study's
subject matter clearly. The first two paragraphs are not sufficiently clear, particularly in
introducing the concept of "big data." It would be beneficial to discuss the characteristic
elements of big data and differentiate between structured, unstructured, and semistructured data. This is crucial for readers to grasp the subject thoroughly. For reference,
see Jonathan Grossman and Ami Pedahzur, [Ref:1]
Clarification of concepts: The sentence ‘data “is the new oil and lifeblood of economic
development” and just as oil needs to be burnt for it to be useful, raw data must be
processed to realise its true potential’ is problematic and contested. This analogy
oversimplifies the complexities of data processing in the digital economy. See, e.g., Clemens
Mewald, ‘Why Data Is *Not* the New Oil and Data Marketplaces Have Failed Us’ (Medium,
13 July 2023) [external resource identifier omitted] David Moschella, ‘Data Isn’t the New Oil; That
Might Be a Good Thing’ (2023) [external resource identifier omitted]




2) Regulatory Framework
A broader perspective is needed: The paper should more comprehensively address the regulatory
challenges of TDM, particularly from a data protection standpoint. This includes not only the
technical challenges of big data processing but also the legal issues associated with scraping and
mining of publicly available data. Including opinions from public agencies and supervisory bodies
would offer a more holistic view of the regulatory landscape. These perspectives could be
instrumental in identifying the main challenges to individual rights and public interests.
3) Data Protection Issues
○

○

○

○

○

Insufficient coverage of GDPR issues: The paper does not sufficiently address the
complexities and challenges that data mining poses for data subjects. The paper relies on
some sources of questionable quality. It would benefit from a more careful selection of
references, particularly those recognised as authoritative in the field. I recommend citing
more reliable sources, especially when describing the fundamental elements of GDPR, such
as Christopher Kuner and others (eds), [Ref:2],A Commentary (New York, 2020; online edn,
Oxford Academic); Indra Spiecker genannt Döhmann and others (eds), General Data
Protection Regulation: Article-by-article Commentary (München, 2023; Beck).
Concept of "meaningful research": The paper should elaborate on the idea of "meaningful
research" and how data protection regulations address data processing for scientific,
research, or statistical purposes. This is a critical aspect that currently needs more depth.
Data Protection by Design and Default: When discussing the implementation of the
principle of data protection by design and default, it is important to reference guidelines
issued by supervisory authorities. For instance, the EDPB Guidelines 4/2019 on Article 25
Data Protection by Design and by Default [Ref 5]; Commission Nationale d’Informatique et
des Libertés (CNIL), GDPR guide for developers (2022); Agencia Española de Protección de
Datos (AEPD), A Guide to Privacy by Design (2019).
Data mining, profiling and inferences: The paper should more comprehensively address the
challenges and risks of data mining, especially concerning profiling and the processing of
inferred data. The relevance of purpose limitation and data minimisation principles needs
more emphasis. Key references include Bart Custers and others (eds), [Ref:3,4]
Missing legal aspects. Data scraping: The paper currently lacks a discussion on the legal
aspects of data scraping at scale and text mining of publicly available data, which are
increasingly relevant, especially for training AI models. It would be beneficial to incorporate
an analysis of the legal challenges posed by these practices, e.g., Benjamin Bremert, Legal
Aspects of Text Mining Publicly Available Data, Unabhängiges Landeszentrum für Datenschutz
(ULD), 2017; Zuzanna Gulczynska, ‘Scraping personal data from internet pages - a
comparative analysis of the Polish Bisnode decision and the US hiQ Labs v LinkedIn Corp
judgment’, European Law Review, vol. 45, no. 6, pp. 857–869, 2020; Catherine Altobelli and
others, ‘To Scrape or Not to Scrape? The Lawfulness of Social Media Crawling under the
GDPR’, in Jean Herveg (ed), Deep Driving into Data Protection: 1979-2019: Celebrating 40 Years
of Privacy and Data Protection at the CRIDS (Larcier, 2021); Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens,
Richtlijnen scraping door private organisaties en particulieren (2024)




4) TDM and fundamental rights
Effectively addressing bias and discrimination in data mining is critical to safeguarding
fundamental rights. Failure to do so can result in inequitable outcomes that disproportionately
harm marginalised groups, perpetuating existing social inequalities. See Bettina Berendt and
Sören Preibusch, ‘Toward Accountable Discrimination-Aware Data Mining: The Importance of
Keeping the Human in the Loop-and Under the Looking Glass’, Big Data. 2017 Jun;5(2):135-152;
Solon Barocas and Andrew Selbst, ‘Big Data's Disparate Impact’, 104 California Law Review 671
(2016); Solon Barocas, ‘Data Mining and the Discourse on Discrimination’, Conference on
Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (2014).
5) Several footnotes and cross-references need to be revised and improved for accuracy and
clarity.

The paper provides a highly valuable overview of the literature on the topic of TDM. Exploring the
literature in a meaningful manner and highlighting scholarly work conducted on this topic.
The following comments and suggestions are submitted for the author’s consideration:
Methodology
The sources included in the review are mostly relevant and the analysis is sound however some
aspects of the methodology section would benefit from further development:
1. The sources selected consist mostly of well-known authors and reputable publication
venues. However, the characteristics of journals or other venues of publications either were
not considered or are not described. Given the proliferation of low-quality, biased or
otherwise unreliable publications, it should be addressed whether or not the study included
a qualitative approach to the selection of sources, and if relevant how.
2. Table 1 categorizes the literature by topics (most of them of a legal nature), however, some
of the sources appear to present other disciplinary perspectives. It is unclear whether the
field of research of the literature analyzed was considered and how such influenced the
qualitative analysis of the materials.
3. A large part of the literature analyzed is legal literature where the jurisdictional aspect is
relevant, the methodology section does not clearly state the jurisdictional focus of the study
and whether comparative law or other methodologies were used in the qualitative analysis.
Instead, the section ‘jurisdictional variance’ provides some information in this regard which
could be more detailed.
4. Arguably, there is a strong possibility that a considerable body of legal literature has been
published in the official languages of each jurisdiction, in particular in those countries that
have enacted national legislation on TDM that predates Directive (EU) 2019/790 CDSM.
However, the literature reviewed only included publications in the English language. If
language was a selection factor it should be described and treated as an important
methodological limitation or has a subject scope delimitation.
Readability
1. The text is well written with occasional less clear sentences. Some sentences and
paragraphs are excessively long and complex.
2. The use of the plural ‘they’ to avoid gender pronouns can be confusing. Gender neutrality is
important and can be better achieved with the person's name or neutral expressions, such
as ‘the author’ or equivalent.
3. A few footnotes require revision and the entries in the appendix are inconsistently cited,
with many being incomplete.
These points can easily be improved with the usual final text review, which is recommended.
Substantive content
1.Section ‘Regulatory frameworks which govern TDM'
Would benefit from a clear structure and a definition of what is understood by “lawful TDM”. The
term lawful entails a presumption of compliance with a set of legal rules, thus it should be
accompanied by clear specification of the said set of rules (including eventual conditions and




exceptions).
2. Section ‘TDM and Intellectual Property Rights’
The section does not address all IPRs, perhaps it would benefit from being more accurately named
or at least the type of IPRs considered could be enunciated in the section's introductory sentences.
Some statements in the text are excessively vague or not sufficiently explored/supported. For
example, the statement below introduces several points of comparative law that are left ‘hanging
in the air’, and are not explored further in the section. I would suggest either erasing ( ‘kill the
darling’) or further elaborating.
‘Jackson Bertón, who examined the applicable copyright frameworks of the five largest economies
of South America in a pre-CDSM era, claimed that even then, the EU was falling behind other more
competitive jurisdictions, but ultimately found that South American frameworks were not
prepared for digital research techniques.’
3. Section ‘ TDM and Data Protection’
Here the reader faces difficulties with the jurisdictional aspect. Although the information is
implied, it should be made more clear what is the jurisdictional origin and coverage of the legal
instruments mentioned (e.g. GDPR). It is not always clear what jurisdiction was considered in the
papers analysed.
Some of the papers analysed in this section were written in the early 2000’s. The temporal aspect
could be better scrutinized as to whether their findings remain unchanged by subsequent
technological and legal developments.
4. Section ‘TDM and Fundamental Rights’
What is understood by fundamental rights and what legal framework(s) are considered is not
defined. The expressions ‘fundamental rights’, ‘human rights’ and ‘fundamental human rights’ are
sometimes used interchangeably making those sentences confusing.
5.Section ‘Generalist approach’
The qualification of the papers analysed under this section as ‘generalist’ is not very convincing.
Perhaps the author could better justify their classification, or otherwise include this literature in
previous sections.

This is a very relevant piece of research reviewing the literature in the field of TDM. As such it is
important and, within the limits of the initial stage of the research project, original and well
developed. A few observations can be found below that may be taken into considerations by the
author in the next stages.
"Lawful tdm": not clear what it is, lacks definition.
Literature review: not clear in which disciplinary domains it was conducted. Are you assessing
mainly legal sources, or also technical literature (computer science; digital humanities, etc)? There
seems to be a need to define better the boundaries of the review and which concepts are
assumed.
“Some scholars make a distinction between text mining and data mining.18 Whilst this distinction
may be vital on the technical side of TDM, altering the analysis techniques used, it arguably does
not necessarily play a pivotal role in the regulatory frameworks which may apply. Data mining is
sometimes seen as a subset of text mining since text mining is the computational process of
analysing unstructured messy data, whilst data mining is the computational process of analysing
structured data.19 “
General observation: It is not always clear where you are reviewing current literature and where
you are taking a position in the debate. This should be made clearer. As a lit. rev. I would assume
the former, but I have doubts here and there.
E.g.,: One could of course argue that text is more copyright focused, while data is less copyright
and, if applicable, more sgdr/neighbouring rights with different regulatory impact. Is this
something that you are addressing?




Lit rev. may need to be temporally structured: e.g., sources of 2022-2024 are discussed together
with sources of 2014 (e.g., around fn 20 – 25 but also in other parts), but the underlying
technology and regulatory framework have evolved considerably. Are there category
commensurate?
“Bearing in mind the definition of TDM presented above” why not using the CDSM definition?
“One of these solutions, Manteghi claims could be found under Article 35 of the proposed Data Act
which “provides a safe harbour for users needing to access, use or share only databases made of data
generated by the use of a product or related service (IoT data)”.83“
Unclear. Perhaps clarify that Art. 43 (ex 35) Data Act, only refers to SGDR not copyright.
“On the other hand, Kretschmer et al., who examined machine learning, natural language
processing and computer vision for computer moderation as case studies where TDM is vital,
found that legal uncertainties like those created by fair use exceptions, can lead to practices
exploiting these uncertainties for commercial gain, particularly by large tech corporations.“
Same as above.
General observation: It seems that certain statements are somehow decontextualised from the
original source and used in a way that changes the meaning. In the specific example above, it
seems that Kretschmer is against fair use for tdm. If I recall it correctly, they are in favour,
however, they suggest that legal uncertainty (which can be found in various legal mechanisms
including fair use) has, among its consequences, that of favouring larger players who have the
financial resources to litigate/resist in court.
It may be necessary to revise that all the excerpts are correctly contextualised in order to ensure
that the cited literature is assessed properly.
The part on fundamental right seems a bit rushed in comparison to copyright and DP and to
conflate EU/US?
The “generalist approach” category and section is not clear. How is it different from the sections
analysed above, particularly copyright? It also seems to rediscuss some of the same sources
already analysed.

Conclusions: again it seems you are expressing an opinion about TDM, but can you do that on the
basis of a lit. rev.? Perhaps, at this stage you should only focus on what emerges from lit. rev.
(which you do in part at the end of the section).

Thank you very much for your constructive and insightful comments. I have thoroughly
revised the paper in light of your feedback, and I believe these changes have significantly
strengthened the review. Below, I address each of your comments and explain the
adjustments made.
1. Introduction: Structure and Clarity
I have restructured the introduction to improve clarity. The concept of "big data" is now
introduced with a more thorough explanation of its characteristic elements, including a
clearer distinction between structured and unstructured data. I have also reconsidered the
analogy of data being “the new oil,” and, following your advice, I have removed such
statements.
1. Regulatory Framework: Broader Perspective
The section on the regulatory framework has been expanded to offer a broader and more
comprehensive discussion of the legal challenges associated with TDM, particularly from a
data protection standpoint. I have added references to opinions from public agencies and
supervisory bodies to provide a more holistic view of the regulatory landscape. Data
Protection Issues: More Depth and Careful Source Selection The data protection section
has been substantially reworked to include more authoritative and recognised sources, as
you recommended. Additionally, I have expanded on the concept of "meaningful research,"
elaborating on how data protection regulations address the processing of data for scientific,
research, or statistical purposes. I have also incorporated references to the EDPB Guidelines
4/2019 on Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and Default), as you suggested. Data
Mining, Profiling, and Inferences I have significantly expanded the discussion on the
challenges and risks of data mining, particularly regarding profiling and the processing of
inferred data. Legal Aspects of Data Scraping I have added a paragraph discussing the
legal aspects of data scraping citing the sources that you had recommended.
1. Fundamental Rights: Bias and Discrimination
I have reworked the section on fundamental rights to more thoroughly address
the critical issues of bias and discrimination in data mining.
2. Footnotes and Cross-References
I have revised the footnotes and cross-references to improve their accuracy
and clarity. This includes correcting any inconsistencies and ensuring that all
references are properly cited and linked to the relevant sections of the paper.
Once again, thank you for your detailed feedback. I am confident that the revisions made in
response to your comments have strengthened the paper both in terms of structure and
substantive content.

Thank you for your constructive feedback, which has been invaluable in helping me to
strengthen this literature review. I have carefully addressed each of your comments and
made the necessary revisions to the paper. Below, I provide a detailed response to your
suggestions.
1. Methodology: Selection Criteria and Language Limitation
I have clarified the selection criteria for the literature included in this review. The
introduction now explicitly discusses the section criteria used. I have also acknowledged
that the study focused on publications in English due to the scope of the review, and I have
identified this as a methodological limitation. Additionally, I have noted the possibility that
significant legal literature may exist in other languages, particularly in countries with preexisting TDM legislation, and this is now treated as a subject scope limitation.
1. Use of ‘They’ and Readability
Following your suggestion, I have replaced the use of the plural ‘they’ with specific
references to ‘the author’ or the author's name to avoid confusion. I have also restructured
several sections, shortening complex and overly long sentences to improve readability and
clarity. A review of the footnotes has been conducted to correct inconsistencies, and the
appendix has been updated to ensure all entries are complete and correctly cited.
1. Definition of “Lawful TDM” in Regulatory Frameworks Section
I have revised the section on regulatory frameworks to include a clearer definition of “lawful
TDM.” The term is now defined as “TDM that is considered compliant with applicable
regulatory frameworks”. This should make the concept more transparent for the reader.
1. TDM and Intellectual Property Rights Section
Based on your feedback, I have renamed the section ‘TDM and Intellectual Property Rights’
to ‘TDM and Copyright and Related Rights’ to better reflect its content. Furthermore, I have
removed the portions that you suggested did not add sufficient value to the discussion,
such as the statement regarding Jackson Bertón’s analysis of South American copyright
frameworks. This has helped to eliminate vague or unsupported statements, ensuring the
section remains focused and well-supported.
1. Fundamental Rights Section
I have revised the section on TDM and Fundamental Rights to clarify what is meant by
fundamental rights. The introductory paragraphs now define the legal frameworks
considered, and I have ensured that the terms ‘fundamental rights’, ‘human rights’, and
‘fundamental human rights’ are used consistently to avoid confusion. This should provide a
more structured and coherent discussion.
1. Generalist Approach Section
I have revisited the ‘Generalist Approach’ section, and I now provide a clearer justification




for the classification of the papers analysed under this category. I explain why they are
considered ‘generalist’ in their approach to TDM, distinguishing this category from other
sections of the review. Once again, thank you for your insightful suggestions. These
revisions have contributed significantly to improving the clarity, structure, and overall
quality of the paper.

Thank you for your valuable feedback. I have carefully considered each of your comments
and made revisions accordingly to improve the clarity and strength of the paper. Below, I
provide a point-by-point response to your suggestions.
1. "Lawful TDM" is unclear, lacks definition:
I have now briefly defined “lawful TDM” as “TDM which would be considered compliant with
the applicable regulatory frameworks” in the relevant section, ensuring that this term is
clearer for the reader.
1. Literature review: disciplinary domains unclear:
I have clarified in the introduction that no disciplinary boundaries were imposed in the
selection criteria for the literature reviewed, to reflect the interdisciplinary nature of TDM.
This literature spans legal, technical, and policy domains. This revision aims to better
communicate the broad scope of the review.
1. Clarification of position vs. review:
I have made clearer distinctions between my own interpretations and the positions found in
the literature. Where I offer commentary, it is now more clearly framed as a response or
evaluation of the literature, rather than presenting it as a standalone position. This is
particularly important for a literature review, and I appreciate your observation in this
regard.
1. Temporal structuring of the literature:
Although I have chosen not to temporally structure the review, I have made it clearer when
older sources are discussed alongside newer ones. I have provided explicit justification for
the inclusion of these older sources, explaining why their contributions remain relevant
despite technological and regulatory developments.
1. Use of CDSM definition:
I have revised the relevant section to incorporate the CDSM definition of TDM, as you
suggested. This revision ensures greater coherence with existing EU legal frameworks.




1. Clarification regarding Article 43 (formerly Article 35) of the Data Act:
I have clarified that Article 43 (formerly 35) of the Data Act refers specifically to SGDR, not
copyright, as you rightly pointed out.
1. Contextualisation of Kretschmer et al.'s position on fair use:
I have revisited the discussion of Kretschmer et al.'s work to ensure that it is accurately
contextualised. The revision better reflects their nuanced position on fair use, highlighting
their concern about legal uncertainty benefiting larger players, while also ensuring that
their general support for fair use is not misrepresented.
1. Fundamental rights section and conflation of US/EU perspectives:
I have revised the fundamental rights section to avoid conflating EU and US perspectives.
The revision now presents these frameworks more distinctly.
1. Generalist approach and redundancy in the review:
I have restructured the “generalist approach” section to avoid redundancy, ensuring that it
builds upon prior sections rather than repeating the same sources or arguments. I have
clarified how it differs from the copyright-focused discussions, making the overall structure
of the paper more coherent.
1. Conclusions:
I have revised the conclusion to ensure that it focuses strictly on summarising the key
findings from the literature review. I have removed any personal opinions or evaluative
commentary that could be construed as going beyond the scope of a literature review.
Thank you once again for your insightful comments, which have contributed significantly to
refining the paper.

Abstract
Text and data mining (TDM) is a process, typically automated, that
looks for patterns in data that may otherwise remain unnoticed. In a
world where data driven solutions play a progressively more
important role, TDM has become a vital tool in sectors ranging from
medicine, to commerce, gaining widespread attraction. Nevertheless,
a variety of regulatory frameworks not always specifically attuned
towards regulating TDM continue to apply concurrently. The literature
within the context of regulatory frameworks governing TDM is a
fragmented piecemeal of valuable insights into what “lawful” TDM
resembles.
This literature review adopts a grounded theory approach analysing
88 pieces of literature, collating views regarding “lawful” TDM,
ultimately providing a holistic assessment of academics’ and
practitioners’ views and opinions regarding the regulatory framework
which governs TDM. A total of 7 categories were identified and each of
these are analysed. Tables are provided in the Appendix (accessible
here: [external resource identifier omitted] which
scholarly works were used for each section of the literature review,
but also how those works were used.
It is ultimately concluded that the regulatory frameworks that apply to
users conducting TDM are multifaceted, and ever-changing on a caseby-case basis. There is an ever-growing need for a holistic
interpretation of the regulatory frameworks which apply, creating a
map which would allow for users conducting TDM to navigate this
complex web of legal rules.
Plain language abstract
Text and data mining (TDM) is an automated method used to find
hidden patterns in information and is often used to generate new
knowledge. TDM is used widely today but the laws that apply to TDM
are unclear. Similarly, research examining the laws that apply to TDM
offer snippets of valuable insights.

This paper examines 88 pieces of literature which study the laws that
apply to TDM, providing a more complete image of academics’ views
on this topic.
What this paper shows is that the laws for people doing TDM are
complicated and change depending on the situation. There is a
growing need for a complete understanding of these laws, to help
people doing TDM find their way through this tricky set of laws.

One of the most influential regulatory frameworks in this regard
is the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).124 As
per Lynskey, unlike jurisdictions like the US, which is characterised as having a “sectoral” regulation of data protection
and privacy, meaning certain aspects of data protection and
privacy are regulated on a granular level, the GDPR takes an
“omnibus” approach towards the all-encompassing regulation of data protection and privacy.125 Under Article 2, the
GDPR regulates the processing of personal data.126 As such “to
fully understand the material scope, one needs to look at the
definitions of “personal data”, [and] “processing”.”127
Article 4(1) defines personal data as “any information relating to
an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an
identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly
or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such
as a name, an identification number, location data, an online
identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical,
physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social

identity of that natural person”.128 The notion of “any information,” implies that the term “personal data” should be interpreted
as broadly as possible.129 Similarly, the CJEU in case
C-434/16, stated that the notion of “relating to” found under
Article 4(1) of the GDPR is “is satisfied where the information, by reason of its content, purpose or effect, is linked to a
particular person”.130 As per Bygrave and Tosoni, this “puts
another gaping hole in the few borders of the personal data concept, although the reference to ‘a particular person’ would seem
to exclude that data relating to an aggregate of persons (e.g.
a household) are personal data, irrespective of the size of the
aggregate”.131 Hence the concept of “personal data” is arguably rather broad. One must also consider the higher level of
protection afforded to so called “special categories of personal data” under Article 9 of the GDPR which restricts the
processing of “personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin,
political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade
union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person,
data concerning health or data concerning a natural person’s
sex life or sexual orientation”.132 This may prove particularly
challenging for users conducting TDM, particularly where
inferences can be made using particular data.133 The GDPR
implications caused to users conducting TDM by inferences
are discussed below.

operations which is performed on personal data or on sets of
personal data, whether or not by automated means, such as collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, adaptation
or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by
transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available,
alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction”.134

are processed” (Article 5(1)(e)), “processed in a manner that
ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including
protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and
against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate
